content.thinking:
I'm tracing the timeline: the monthly-spend-feature flag was enabled at 16:31, triggering ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py, then reverted around 16:38 by Argus — checking the exact timestamps to see if the "refuted" judgment actually holds up against this sequence.

The timing is tight here — T21 checked just 5 seconds after the revert and saw the service still at incident level, then waited up to 120s before marking it refuted at 16:40:16. But the Gce95 logs still show flag=on evaluations occurring through 16:39, after the provider recorded the flag switching off at 16:38:02, which suggests the service may not have actually picked up the revert. I shouldn't over-claim this though — the record itself says refuted, so I need to focus on where the candidate and record actually disagree.

Since the revert was refuted, the trigger isn't fully confirmed, so I'm building the chain carefully: the symptom is account pages failing (Gbac1, G5309), traced to requests raising a ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47, which per F1 only happens when the flag path is enabled for a shopper with no purchases this month.

The flag turned on at 16:31 (P1), matching when errors began, with G971b and Gce95 showing it evaluated on afterward. But the revert attempt (M1, T19-T22) didn't fix the service, and the logs actually still show the flag evaluating on at 16:39—even after it was supposedly switched off at 16:38:02 (P2)—so I can't honestly claim the service ran with the flag off during the check.

The logs span roughly 16:29 to 16:39, likely covering part of that final minute. The causal chain points to the division-by-zero issue tied to shoppers without purchases, rooted in the flag flip at P1 — no other deploys or changes show up in the record to compete with that as the trigger, even though the revert itself was judged refuted.

I need to be honest here: the flag's tie to the incident isn't fully confirmed since the revert was refuted, yet the error pattern at line 47, timing, and log evaluations all point to the flag being on, and logs suggest the service kept treating it as on even after the revert. I'll word the causal step to reflect that nuance rather than overstating certainty, since the chain's reasoning rests on an unrun F1 check for the empty list division.

I also want to confirm what else was ruled out — deploys showed no returns, replicas are all one revision, and only Argus made a flag change in that hour per the provider logs, so other flag changes are excluded. There was an earlier unrelated incident that tried reverting the same flag and got refuted, which is worth noting but isn't itself a ruled-out cause.

Now I'm thinking about contributing factors: no test appeared to cover the flag-enabled path for a shopper with zero purchases this month before the flag was turned on, which the fix addresses by adding tests; and the flag was switched on for a large chunk of traffic at once rather than gradually.

Looking at the eval logs, the flag went from off to on for all 200 evaluations within a single minute, meaning there was no staged rollout — everyone got the new behavior essentially at once. Another factor to consider is whether anyone was actually paged for this, since the alert doesn't seem to link to an on-call incident.

I'm also seeing that the revert didn't take effect immediately — the service was still evaluating the flag as "on" at 16:39 even after it was supposedly switched off, suggesting some kind of propagation delay or caching issue that held before the incident began.

That goes under went_wrong, and still_at_risk should note the flag remains on, so shoppers with no purchases this month keep failing account pages. I also notice the premature 5-second check at T21 isn't a real issue since it waited afterward, but the fact that T16 had the same refuted revert on the same flag suggests this is a recurring, unfixed problem.

Detection timing checks out fine — alert fired about 14 seconds after the expected window, nothing to flag there. For went_well, I'm crediting Argus for picking up the incident promptly, the investigator for correctly matching onset to the flag change, the revert action, and Code-Fix for proposing the draft PR quickly. The tricky part is how to frame putting the flag back ON — it's reversible and matches the designed response, but the logs show the service still evaluating it as on during the check, so that nuance belongs under went_wrong rather than went_well.

I don't see any clear "got lucky" factor here — nothing suggests the fault was contained by chance rather than design, so I'll leave that section empty. For the symptom line, I'm settling on something concise like "Account pages failed to load for many shoppers."

Now I'm building out the causal chain: account page error rates spiked and peaked, traced to a ZeroDivisionError at a specific line in spend_summary.py starting at 16:31, caused by dividing this month's spend by zero purchases for shoppers who bought previously but not this month, with the render path only reaching that line under specific conditions.

I'm tracing that condition to the monthly-summary feature flag, which an admin switched on at a specific timestamp — the service began evaluating it as on from that moment, having evaluated it off before. I'm ruling out deploys and other flag changes as causes since none occurred in the relevant window, but I'm flagging a caveat: a later revert attempt is judged refuted, since logs still show the service evaluating the flag as on in the following minutes even after the provider recorded it switched off — meaning there's no evidence the service ever actually measured behavior with the flag off again after that revert. I'm deciding how to phrase this nuance carefully so the chain doesn't incorrectly assert the revert actually took effect.

The root cause itself: a function computing average spend per item for the current month divides total spend by purchase count without guarding against zero purchases, so a shopper who bought previously but not this month triggers a division by zero — and this code path is only reachable once the monthly-spend feature flag is enabled, which explains why the account page failed. I'm being careful to label any numeric references like line numbers as placeholder markers rather than writing raw figures directly, while leaving labels like PR numbers untouched since they're identifiers rather than quantities.

For the "still at risk" assessment, since the flag got re-enabled and the division logic was never fixed, the account page is likely still failing for any shopper with prior purchases but none this month. I'm also considering a follow-up action item to investigate why the service evaluated the flag as on shortly after it was recorded off, though I'm unsure yet whether to tie it to an existing concern or leave it unlinked.

Other mitigation ideas come to mind too: staged rollout of flags like monthly-spend-feature to a small percentage of traffic with an error-rate gate before widening further, filed as a prevent item under CF-2. I'm also thinking about paging routing for HighErrorRate alerts.

I'm also considering requiring tests on a flag's newly-enabled path before it can be flipped on in production as a process safeguard for CF-1, though AI-1 may already cover this via PR tests. Checking the rollout data, I see G971b went live at 16:31 with 89 on versus 111 off within that minute, while Gce95 flipped fully on starting 16:32 with 200 events — suggesting the rollout wasn't gradual for the second flag.

I should flag the key assumptions: that shoppers affected are those who purchased before but not this month comes purely from reading the code, not the logs; and that the flag evaluated as "on" after the revert is inferred from per-minute aggregates rather than exact timestamps, since the records don't show precisely when within the 16:39 minute that occurred.

For went_wrong, I won't repeat that nobody paged since that's a contributing factor already captured elsewhere. I'm noting that an earlier incident involving the same flag's revert was found and apparently repeated. For went_well, I'm crediting Argus for picking up the incident shortly after the alert fired, and the investigator for correctly pinpointing the onset time.

For went_wrong, the revert of the flag was judged as refuted and put back on, but the logs still show the service treating monthly-spend-feature as active at 16:39, suggesting the fix didn't actually take effect.

I'm also noting that deploy-related causes were ruled out since no deploys came back in the search, while flag changes T15 and T36 are worth citing.

For contributing factors, I'm listing a few counterfactuals: a missing test for the flag-on path with a zero-purchase shopper could have caught this before rollout, the lack of a staged rollout meant the flag hit all requests at once instead of a limited share, and the absence of a page meant no one was actively watching when the revert check was refuted. I want to phrase the PR reference carefully to avoid stray bare numbers, maybe using "the draft pull request" instead of the literal identifier.

action_items.item: Find out why io-shop kept evaluating monthly-spend-feature as on in the minute after the flag provider recorded it switched off.
Switch monthly-spend-feature off again until the fix in PR #376 is merged.
Roll monthly-spend-feature, and flags like it, out to a small share of requests first, with an error-rate gate before the share is widened.
Require tests that cover a flag's newly enabled code path before the flag can be switched on in production.
Link the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to an on-call page so that a person is paged when it fires.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed. The share of io-shop requests answered with a server error rose from {errors_before} before the onset to {errors_while_broken} while it was broken, and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. The service's own account-page error-rate warnings peaked at {Gbac1.5}.

Why did they fail? From the onset minute on, account page requests raised ZeroDivisionError at line {F1.1} of src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. These errors are not in the log lines read from before the onset.

Why did that line divide by zero? Code-Fix's reading of the code says `average_spend_per_item_this_month` divides this month's spend by the number of purchases made this month. For a shopper who has bought before but not this month, there are no such purchases, so it divides by zero.

ruled_out.what: A deploy: none came back from either search of production changes.
Any other flag change: in the hour before each read, the flag provider's history showed only one change by anyone but Argus, the switch of monthly-spend-feature.

causal_chain.step: Why was that code reached? Code-Fix's reading says `render_spend_summary` reaches it only when the monthly summary is on, which is what monthly-spend-feature enables. An admin switched monthly-spend-feature on at {P1.1}, the onset minute. The service had evaluated the flag as off in every minute before. In the onset minute it evaluated the flag as on for {G971b.2} of {G971b.3} evaluations, and as on in every minute after that. Reverting the flag was judged refuted. However, the log lines read show the service still evaluating the flag as on, and still failing at the same line, in the {T20.2} minute the check watched. That was after the provider recorded the flag switched off at {P2.1}. So the record does not show the service measured with the flag off.

input.cause_in_plain_words: A newly switched-on feature on the shop's account page likely tried to work out a shopper's average spend per item this month by dividing by the number of items they had bought this month, and that sum cannot be done for shoppers who had bought nothing yet this month, so their pages failed.

contributing_factors.factor: No test was seen of the monthly-summary path for a shopper with purchases before but none this month. Code-Fix's reading adds two such cases to tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py, and both would raise against the current code.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A test like that would have failed on the division before the flag was switched on, and the fault would have been found without reaching shoppers.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: monthly-spend-feature reached every request within a minute of being switched on: from the following minute, every evaluation logged was on. No staged rollout and no error-rate gate on widening the flag were seen.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Turning the flag on for a small share of requests first would have limited failures to that share, and the errors could have been caught before every shopper was exposed.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: Nobody was paged: the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop was not linked to any on-call incident.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A paged person could have taken the incident up when the alert fired, and acted after the flag revert was judged refuted instead of the incident waiting at escalation.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

went_well: Argus took the incident up {T2.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised.
The Investigator placed the onset in the same minute monthly-spend-feature was switched on, and named the failing line from the logs.
The Mitigation Agent reverted monthly-spend-feature, a change that could be put back, {T19.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised.
Code-Fix proposed a draft fix, PR #376, {T39.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised.
went_wrong: The flag revert was judged refuted and monthly-spend-feature was put back on. Yet the log lines read show the service still evaluating the flag as on, and still failing at the same line, in the {T20.2} minute the check watched, after the provider recorded the flag off at {P2.1}. The check may never have seen the service run with the flag off.

input.root_cause: In src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, `average_spend_per_item_this_month` divides the shopper's spend this month by the number of purchases flagged in the current month and does not handle an empty list. For a shopper who has bought before but not this month, it raises ZeroDivisionError at line {F1.1}. The account page reaches this function only on the monthly-summary path that monthly-spend-feature enables, and the exception fails the whole account page request.
input.still_at_risk: monthly-spend-feature had been put back on and the division was unchanged, so the account page would likely keep failing for any shopper who has bought before but not this month.
input.symptom: Account pages failed to load for many shoppers
